justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for gold prices across all three horizons, starting near what I assessed as the prevailing spot price around $1,930 per ounce and drifting slightly higher over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate stays close to current levels because intraday momentum and overnight positioning rarely produce large directional moves in the absence of a scheduled catalyst. Over one week, I nudged the estimate up slightly to reflect a mild tailwind from persistent safe-haven demand, dollar uncertainty, and ongoing central bank buying trends that have characterized the gold market in recent periods. At one month, the further drift higher captures a continuation of those same macro forces — particularly expectations around Federal Reserve policy pivots, geopolitical tensions, and real yield dynamics — while acknowledging that the direction of travel for gold over medium-term horizons has leaned constructive.

The confidence interval widths widen considerably as the horizon extends, which is standard for any asset with sensitivity to macro surprises. At one day, the interval is relatively tight because the dominant drivers are technical and positioning-based, with limited scheduled news that would cause a breakout. At one week, the interval widens to reflect the possibility of a surprise inflation print, a Fed speaker comment, or a geopolitical escalation shifting sentiment materially. At one month, the range becomes quite wide because the cumulative probability of a meaningful macro shock — a hard landing signal, a dollar rally, an unexpected rate decision, or a risk-on surge that diverts flows from gold — grows substantially.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals entirely. On the upside, a sudden escalation in a major geopolitical conflict, a significant banking stress event, or an unexpectedly dovish Fed pivot could send gold sharply above the upper bounds of even the one-month interval. A genuine flight-to-safety episode of the kind seen in early 2020 or March 2023 could add hundreds of dollars quickly. On the downside, a stronger-than-expected U.S. labor market or inflation re-acceleration could force markets to reprice rate cuts out of the curve, lifting real yields and pressuring gold well below the lower bound. A broad risk-on rally driven by positive growth surprises could also pull speculative capital out of gold aggressively. These tail scenarios are real and, individually, not negligible in probability, which is part of why even the stated intervals should be treated as approximations rather than hard boundaries.
